conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your oncology team members. I’ll be checking in on you during this admission. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit tired, but okay. My neck still hurts, and I’ve been worried about starting the second round of chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re here for your second cycle of R-ICE chemotherapy, which we’re starting tomorrow. The good news is your last MRI showed the nasopharyngeal mass has shrunk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good to hear. But why are we adding Rituxan this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your recent EBV viral load was elevated. Since you have CVID, your immune system can’t control EBV well, and it may be driving the lymphoma. Rituxan helps target those abnormal B cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. That makes sense. Will it make me feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients feel a little flu-like during the first infusion, but we’ll give you pre-medications to help. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My back’s been aching too—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got an MRI of your lumbar spine today to check. It showed only your known degenerative changes from your prior surgery—no signs of lymphoma spreading there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was scared it might be cancer again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’re being extra cautious because of your history. Your spleen is a bit larger than before, but that’s common with lymphoma activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood counts? Last time I was really low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is low at 1.5, and hemoglobin is 7.5, so we’ll keep an eye on it. We’ll transfuse if your hemoglobin drops below 7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helped me feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also adjusted your diabetes meds. We’re using insulin now instead of your oral meds because steroids can raise blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I forgot I’m on dexamethasone with this chemo. My sugars have been high at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your glucose four times a day and giving insulin as needed. Once you’re home, we’ll restart your glimepiride and metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain? I’m on methadone and dilaudid, but sometimes it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team reviewed your meds. We’re keeping your current doses. Pregabalin was increased last time and seems to be helping with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it has. My headaches are better too—probably from the chemo shrinking the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s a good sign the treatment is working. We’ll keep monitoring with scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’ll start your R-ICE chemo, including Rituxan. It’ll take a few hours. Any questions before we begin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Will I lose my hair again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely, yes. But it will grow back after treatment ends. We can talk about scalp cooling if you’re interested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. I just want to get through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. The nurse will start the infusion now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any nausea or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nauseated, but the ondansetron helps. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your white count is up to 2.0 today, which is improving. We’ll keep giving antibiotics to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on acyclovir and atovaquone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. They help protect you from infections because of your CVID.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my IVIG? When’s my next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get it in clinic in about two weeks. Your last level was good, so we’re keeping it every four weeks as you prefer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not come more often. It’s a long trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow you’ll get intrathecal methotrexate via lumbar puncture to protect your central nervous system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It was uncomfortable, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use fluoroscopy to guide the needle, and you’ll be awake but relaxed. We’ll collect some fluid to check for lymphoma cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel pressure, but we’ll numb the area first. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went smoothly. We gave the methotrexate and sent the fluid for testing. No immediate issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I feel okay—just a little stiff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep you lying flat for a bit to reduce headache risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? That’s great. What about the Neupogen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get your first dose before you leave. You’ll inject it daily at home to help your white count recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done it before. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Continue all your usual meds, including methadone, clonazepam, and your inhaler.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist in a week, and your IVIG is scheduled in two weeks. Call us if you develop fever, severe pain, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I feel like I’m on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep up the strength. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my hearing. It’s still not great since the ear surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. ENT said the tube is in place and the infection is cleared. The hearing loss may be from long-term inflammation, but they’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep using the ofloxacin drops as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m ready to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. Your walker is here, and a nurse will go over your meds one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was our pleasure. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.
